generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, your mindset shows itself most clearly when a result disappoints. A low mark on a piece of work can feel like a verdict on whether you are any good at the subject. A growth mindset reads it differently: as information about a particular skill you can build with practice, rather than a fixed limit on what you can do.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who get the same disappointing mark back on a piece of work they tried hard on.

Student A reads the mark, decides the subject is simply not a strength, and files the work away without reading the comments. The effort felt wasted, so there seems little point going back over it. Nothing changes before the next task. This is a fixed-mindset response: the mark is treated as a verdict on ability.

Student B is just as disappointed, but reads the feedback carefully and notes two things that cost marks. Each one becomes a specific thing to practise next time. The mark still stings, but it has become useful. This is a growth-mindset response: the mark is treated as information about what to do next.

Both students got the same mark. Only Student B let it move their learning forward.
generatedProse.summary: A growth mindset earns its place when a result disappoints. A fixed response reads a poor mark as proof of your limits; a growth response reads it as information about a skill you can build. You can now tell the two responses apart, recognise a growth approach in action, and choose one yourself. The next lesson keeps you going once you have decided to carry on.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's approach a growth-mindset one?

items.text: They turned the feedback into specific things to practise next time.
They were less disappointed by the mark than Student A was.
They decided the subject was simply not a strength.
They filed the work away without reading the comments.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B turned the feedback into specific things to practise, letting the mark move their learning forward.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B did with the mark, beyond how they felt about it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B was growth-minded because they turned the feedback into specific things to practise. The other options describe the fixed response or just a feeling.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
